title: Turning to Azerbaijani gas and US LNG, Turkey seeks to break its reliance on Russian energy
gist: Turkey has cut Russia's share of its gas imports from roughly 64 percent in 2006 to 37 percent in early 2025 by pairing a new fifteen-year, 33 bcm Azerbaijani supply deal with a fivefold expansion of LNG regasification capacity (32 to 161 million cubic meters per day, 2016-2025) and long-term US contracts with Mercuria, Cheniere and ExxonMobil. İlker Sezer argues Azerbaijani pipeline gas plus US LNG could unseat Russia as Turkey's largest supplier during the 2030s, but full decoupling is impossible because no other source can carry Turkish baseload demand.

insights.claim: In May, Ankara and Baku concluded a fifteen-year deal covering 33 billion cubic meters of natural gas, securing Azerbaijani supply to Turkey into the mid-2040s.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: A two-decade demand commitment locks in Caspian volumes and shrinks the addressable market for any competing supplier into Turkey.
insights.locator: Azerbaijan becomes a cornerstone of Ankara’s long-term gas strategy

insights.claim: The Azerbaijani supply is underpinned by the Absheron Phase Two project involving SOCAR, Turkey's state-owned BOTAŞ, ADNOC and TotalEnergies, with a SOCAR official saying half of the new production is earmarked for the Turkish domestic market and the remainder freeing up exports for a supply-starved Europe.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Names the specific upstream project and equity holders whose delivery schedule determines whether Turkish diversification math actually works.
insights.locator: underpinned by landmark production agreements

insights.claim: Azerbaijani gas offers Turkey a combination of competitive pricing and reliable supply, according to former Turkish Energy Minister Ali Riza Alaboyun.

insights.so_what: Price competitiveness, not just security of supply, is the stated driver — meaning Russian discounting has limited defensive power.

insights.claim: Turkish imports from Azerbaijan have nearly doubled over a decade from 6.08 bcm in 2014 to 11.48 bcm, now roughly 22 percent of Turkey's total gas imports.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Establishes the growth rate of the pipeline leg against which Russia's decline must be measured.

themes.theme: Russia's eroding but still dominant share

insights.claim: Russian gas accounted for approximately 63.9 percent of Turkey's total natural gas import mix in 2006, fell to 41 percent by the mid-2020s with volumes of 21.57 bcm, and dipped to 37 percent in early 2025.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: A two-decade decline curve with a specific current level — the base case against which any Gazprom volume recovery should be judged.

insights.claim: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine did not derail Turkish gas imports from Moscow: Russia's market share dipped only temporarily from 44.9 percent in 2021 to 39.5 percent in 2022 before rebounding to 42.3 percent in 2023.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Geopolitical shock alone did not displace Russian volumes — only new infrastructure and contracts did, a lesson for forecasting sanctions impact on energy flows.

insights.claim: Combined Azerbaijani pipeline gas and US LNG could unseat Russia as Turkey's largest gas supplier during the 2030s, leaving Russia a major but no longer dominant player.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Sets a decade-scale timeline for the loss of Gazprom's last large European-adjacent market, relevant to long-dated Russian export revenue assumptions.
insights.locator: If these trends continue

insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: A hard regulatory date that shrinks Gazprom's buyer pool and hands Turkey pricing leverage — a catalyst for renegotiated Turkish contract terms.

themes.theme: US LNG and the regas capacity buildout

insights.claim: Turkey's LNG regasification capacity rose from 32 million cubic meters per day in 2016 to approximately 161 million cubic meters per day in 2025 — a fivefold increase — according to Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Regas capacity, not contracts, is the binding constraint on switching away from pipeline gas; Turkey has removed it.
insights.locator: The scale of this infrastructure boom is staggering

insights.claim: Operating five LNG terminals — two land-based and three floating storage regasification units — Turkey can now import roughly 58 bcm annually in liquefied form, a volume exceeding its entire national gas consumption in 2025.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Import optionality now exceeds total demand, meaning Turkey can theoretically zero out pipeline gas on short notice — a hard credibility floor under its negotiating position.
insights.quote: a volume that exceeds its entire national gas consumption in 2025
insights.locator: Operating five sophisticated LNG terminals

insights.claim: US LNG imports to Turkey surged to 9.19 bcm in 2025, capturing nearly 16 percent of the total import market, up from a virtually negligible 0.52 percent in 2016, according to the Centre for Eastern Studies.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Quantifies how fast a supplier can go from nothing to a sixth of a market once regas infrastructure exists — a template for other pipeline-dependent buyers.
insights.locator: According to the Centre for Eastern Studies

insights.claim: Turkey's US LNG relationship is shifting from volatile spot purchases to long-term contracts: Mercuria and Cheniere Energy deals take effect in 2026 delivering roughly 1.2 bcm and 4 bcm annually, and a ten-year ExxonMobil agreement adds 3.45 bcm per year from 2027.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Named counterparties and start dates give a contracted US export volume ramp into Turkey that can be tracked against liquefaction capacity additions.
insights.locator: Notably, contracts with major suppliers such as the Swiss-based energy firm Mercuria

insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Domestic supply is the third leg of the displacement math and would cut import demand outright rather than reshuffling suppliers.

themes.theme: Why full decoupling is not possible

insights.claim: No single source other than Russia can meet Turkey's baseload energy demand with comparable volume and infrastructure-backed reliability, and Turkish gas consumption is expected to rise to 60-65 bcm per year over the next five years.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Sets a demand growth floor that keeps Russian volumes structurally in the mix regardless of political intent — a caution against pricing in full Turkish decoupling.
insights.locator: Bypassing Moscow altogether remains a distant prospect

insights.claim: LNG is exposed to global market shocks and maritime choke points, illustrated by Pakistan having to buy a spot cargo at its most expensive rate in four years in May after a Qatari shipment was cancelled due to Strait of Hormuz disruption.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Concrete precedent for how fast Middle East chokepoint risk transmits into LNG spot prices for import-dependent buyers.
insights.locator: Following the cancellation of a scheduled shipment from Qatar

insights.claim: Turkey is largely shielded from both spot-market swings and maritime chokepoint risk because its long-term contracts cover volumes and its largest LNG suppliers, the US and Algeria, have direct unimpeded access to the Mediterranean.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Geographic supplier selection, not just contract structure, is what neutralizes Hormuz risk — a screen to apply to other LNG importers.

insights.claim: Iran's potential to serve Turkish and European gas needs hinges entirely on a diplomatic breakthrough between Washington and Tehran, a highly remote scenario in the current climate, according to former Energy Minister Alaboyun.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Removes Iranian gas from realistic supply scenarios, tightening the medium-term balance and raising the value of Azerbaijani and US volumes.

themes.theme: Gas hub ambition and its costs

insights.claim: Turkey's ambition to become a gas hub where gas is priced and traded, not just transmitted, has drawn US and European scrutiny over concerns that a homogenized Turkish blend could obscure the origin of Russian gas and enable sanctions evasion.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: The hub project is a sanctions-integrity risk that could invite Western countermeasures, an underappreciated friction in the Turkish energy story.
insights.locator: Ankara’s energy hub vision complicates its diversification efforts

insights.claim: Turkey has built the physical hub infrastructure — an expanded FSRU fleet and interconnected pipelines — but a genuine financial trading hub still requires deep private-sector involvement, regulatory liberalization, and supply diversity the domestic market has yet to achieve.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Distinguishes infrastructure milestones from market-design milestones — the second set is what would actually create a tradable Turkish price benchmark.

insights.claim: Turkey's diversification should be read as an exercise in maximizing geopolitical leverage rather than total decoupling from Moscow, eroding Russia's ability to use energy as a political tool while keeping it as a supplier.
insights.speaker: İlker Sezer
insights.so_what: Reframes the metric of success from volume displacement to bargaining power — expect Turkish contract renegotiations rather than outright supplier exits.
